{"docket_number": "70-110", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1971", "first_party": "Wisconsin", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "Yoder", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "Wisconsin Supreme Court", "argued": ["1971-12-08T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Did Wisconsin's requirement that all parents send their children to school at least until age 16 violate the First Amendment by criminalizing the conduct of parents who refused to send their children to school for religious reasons?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Jonas Yoder and Wallace Miller, both members of the Old Order Amish religion, and Adin Yutzy, a member of the Conservative Amish Mennonite Church, were prosecuted under a Wisconsin law that required all children to attend public schools until age 16. The three parents refused to send their children to such schools after the eighth grade, arguing that high school attendance was contrary to their religious beliefs.

", "conclusion": "

The Court held that individual's interests in the free exercise of religion under the First Amendment outweighed the State's interests in compelling school attendance beyond the eighth grade. In the majority opinion by Chief Justice Warren E. Burger, the Court found that the values and programs of secondary school were "in sharp conflict with the fundamental mode of life mandated by the Amish religion," and that an additional one or two years of high school would not produce the benefits of public education cited by Wisconsin to justify the law. Justice William O. Douglas filed a partial dissent but joined with the majority regarding Yoder. Justices Lewis Powell and William Rehnquist took no part in the consideration or decision of the case.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Good evening everyone. My name is Troy Mackenzie. I'm the dean of the Law school and I am thrilled to be welcoming you all to the inaugural life of the law event. Before we get underway, there's someone who is really central to this event that I would like to thank, and that's Chris Buck. He is the founder of Retro Report, which is nonprofit news organization that brings together documentary journalism with history and civics education. The goal is to combat misinformation, and one of the things that Retro Report does is to look at the people behind his historical events in order to humanize history and make it relevant for today so you can understand why he has been supportive of this event. So thank you, Chris, for making this possible. I just want to talk a little bit about the concept behind this event. The inspiration for this series comes from the famous quote by Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. Who once said, the life of the law has not been logic. It has been experience. And of course, what Holmes meant by that is law is not just about deducing from a formula. It's about understanding experience. It's about understanding real lives at moments in time and history. Too often, the real distinctively unique stories that make up people's lives get lost in the headlines about Supreme Court decisions. And this evening we're going to talk about people behind the headlines. In a number of cases that many of you have read about in law school over half a century ago, the court issued landmark decisions that school, school-sponsored prayer in public schools were unconstitutional. And also that states could not require parents to educate their children past grade eight when schooling conflicted with the parents' religious beliefs and the effects of those decisions are still very much relevant today. And there's also a lot of nuance behind the doctrine and behind those decisions. And we have the unique opportunity this evening to hear the stories of the victorious parties in those cases with Joshua Prager, who is a Pulitzer Prize finalist, and Josh is the perfect person to lead tonight's discussion For more than 20 years, he has been a writer first for the Wall Street Journal, has written about historical events revealing a number of important hidden things, including the background behind Bobby Thompson's famous Shot Heard Round the World in baseball. He also has worked to shed light on many of our cultural touchstones. His book, the Family Roe, illuminates Unknown Stories and the People Behind Roe v. Wade and offers to the public perhaps an unforeseen glimpse into the debate about abortion, both in the 1960s and seventies as well as today. And that book was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize. He has spoken at a number of venues including giving a very well-received Ted Talk. He was a fellow at Harvard and also a Fulbright Distinguished Chair at Hebrew University. He lives in New Jersey with his wife and family. And I'm happy to note that we will have another life of the law event in the spring semester where he will interview other families involved in high profile cases before the Supreme Court. And at this time, I would like to turn things over to Josh who will introduce tonight's speakers whom he will be interviewing, and this is going to be an amazing event. So thank you. All right. Thank you so much, Dean Mackenzie. It really is an honor to be here. I have been in this room before for some beautiful events, most recently to honor Judge Katzman and Judge Katzman's wife, Jennifer Callahan is here. So it's exciting for me to be back here and to think of Hammond to see you here. Thank you. And I want to first say that Chris and I have known each other for many, many years, and we've talked about collaborating over the years. So it's exciting to finally have the opportunity to do that. We have a shared interest in history and in sort of looking back at history and finding kind of unknown things about it, but we really needed to find a special partner and to have NYU Law School as that partner is more than I could have imagined. Trevor Morrison, who is sort of joining us this evening on the wall behind us, he really was the person who had the thought that this might be a good home.
